html:
The Golden Bull of 1082 was a trade and defence treaty in which Emperor Alexios I Komnenos gave the Republic of Venice sweeping trading rights in the Byzantine Empire. It was issued as a chrysobull, a decree sealed with gold. Some historians date it to 1092 instead.

Alexios needed the Venetian fleet against the Normans of Robert Guiscard, who had beaten him at Dyrrhachium. In return Venetian merchants could trade almost everywhere in the empire free of customs duties, which Byzantine merchants still paid. Venice also got a quarter of Constantinople on the Golden Horn, with warehouses and wharves, and its doge got an honorary title.

The deal made Venice rich and launched its trading empire in the east. It also bred resentment as Italians came to dominate the empire's trade. Later emperors tried to limit it or played Venice off against Genoa and Pisa, which led to the arrest of the Venetians in 1171 and fed the bitterness behind the sack of 1204.
